$comment: Declared unreachable surfaces, with a WRITTEN REASON for each. Enforced by
tools/check_reachability.py (CI job 'Reachability - nothing implemented-and-uncalled').
Unreachable is sometimes exactly correct: a capability-denied command MUST have no caller,
and a superseded sibling legitimately outlives its last call site. What hides a defect is
unreachable-AND-undeclared - the state in which nobody can tell which of those it is. So
this file is the point of the gate, not an escape hatch from it: every entry costs a
sentence that a reviewer can disagree with, and 'unreachable, no reason given' is refused
by the gate itself (see MIN_REASON_CHARS / PLACEHOLDER_REASONS).
Adding an entry is a claim. If the command later gains a real caller, the gate turns RED
and asks you to DELETE the entry - deliberately, so an exception cannot silently outlive
the condition it described.
`rust_symbols` covers apps/desktop/src-tauri/** the same way `engine_symbols` covers the
python engine. It needs `module` as well as `defined_in`, because a Rust caller must NAME
the symbol (`module::name(`): a bare-name scan would count any unrelated function of the
same name as a caller, and names like `create_schema` / `resolve` / `sweep` are shared by
half a dozen sibling modules in brops-core. rustc never warns about an uncalled `pub fn`
in a library crate, which is why this whole class was invisible here until 2026-08-09.
`rust_symbols` holds SIX entries as of 2026-08-12, in three groups, and the distinction between
them is the point. TWO are the ai-side halves of the 4.10(f) desktop pull that are still unreached
(governed_pull_output, governed_turn_output_read). THREE are
the §4.10(g) submit-frame writer (governed_prepare::prepare_governed_turn_v1b,
::resolve_governed_generation_config_v1b, governed_submit::governed_turn_submit_prepared) - built,
tested, and deliberately not wired, because wiring it would move the shipped broker off its
fail-closed executor. And ONE, `governed_output_pull::pull_output`, is now must_have_caller rather
than declared_unreachable: on 2026-08-12 the live §4.10(f) pull driver
(apps/desktop/src-tauri/core/src/bin/ladder_output_pull.rs) gave it a real named caller, and this
gate's own message says to flip rather than excuse. That caller is a CI PROOF, not a product path;
the gate cannot tell those apart, so the entry says so in prose and the two production blockers it
used to record are written there rather than deleted with it.
TWO entries were DELETED in that same change - governed_bridge_result::parse and ::check_echoes -
because the pull driver calls both and NEITHER call is one this gate can see: `parse` is reached as
the inherent `BridgeTurnResult::parse(` and `check_echoes` as the method `.check_echoes(`, while the
gate matches `module::name(`. They could not be flipped to must_have_caller (that would go RED on a
caller that exists), and leaving them declared_unreachable would have been a declaration that had
become false while the gate stayed green. That is the same hand-deletion, for the same blind spot,
as `parse_frame` earlier the same day - and it is worth restating that a stale declared_unreachable
on live code is the one failure this file cannot be trusted to catch.
2026-08-12, later the same day: the bridge SPAWN moved from apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/ai.rs into
apps/desktop/src-tauri/core/src/governed_sidecar.rs, together with the trust environment it applies
(core/src/engine_trust.rs). None of the entries below changed expectation as a result. Two things
about this gate are worth recording. First, the new seam is reached as an INHERENT associated call
- `GovernedSidecar::as_calling_principal(` from ai.rs and `GovernedSidecar::as_distinct_principal(`
from broker/src/main.rs (it was a single `GovernedSidecar::new(` until 2026-08-12, when the 2.6
principal became a constructor-level choice) - together with `.round_trip(`, the blind spot named
below - so if any of them were
ever declared here, the declaration could go stale without turning the gate red. Second,
`SubmitTransport for GovernedSidecar` is a trait impl with no constructor of its own; a trait impl
cannot be expressed in `rust_symbols` at all, so the fact that it is reachable only through
governed_turn_submit_prepared (which has no caller) is recorded in that entry's prose rather than
enforced here. Neither is a hole this change opened; both are the gate's stated limits, restated
where they now apply.
A SIXTH pull-side entry, governed_bridge_result::parse_frame, was DELETED on 2026-08-12 when
governed_turn_submit_prepared gave it a real production caller. That deletion was made by hand rather
than forced by the gate, and the gap is worth naming: the gate matches `module::name(`, and an
inherent associated call reads as `BridgeTurnResult::parse_frame(`, so it would have stayed green on a
declaration that had become false. A stale `declared_unreachable` on live code is the one failure this
file cannot be trusted to catch, which is why an entry costs a sentence somebody has to keep true.
Reasons: capability-denied | superseded | governed-wall | backend-only | not-yet-wired.
'not-yet-wired' is an honest OPEN gap and must name where it is tracked.
Observed state recorded 2026-08-07 on branch wave/phase-push-1; the gate re-derives it on
every run rather than trusting these notes.

decide_approval.note: The generic approve verb is DENIED to the main window in capabilities/default.json (deny-decide-approval, T-011): approving must require a renderer-independent native confirmation, so a compromised webview cannot approve anything. Having no caller is the ENFORCED state, not an oversight - apps/desktop/src/features/approvalsAuthority.ts names it only as DENIED_DECIDE_COMMAND, a constant that exists so the page can assert it never renders a control for it. The reachable approve path is confirm_approval; the fail-safe path is reject_approval.
decide_approval.observed: 2026-08-07: no invoke; one non-call mention as DENIED_DECIDE_COMMAND in features/approvalsAuthority.ts.

post_message.note: Superseded by post_user_message for every renderer path (P1-6): post_user_message fixes the role server-side, so the webview cannot choose it, while post_message only VALIDATES the role against WEBVIEW_MESSAGE_ROLES = ["user"]. services/desktop.ts exposes postMessage(), which invokes post_user_message. post_message is therefore the WIDER of the two - it accepts a role and checks it, where the superseding command never lets the webview name one at all - and it stays registered and allow-granted with nothing calling it. That is residual invokable surface with no user; flipping its grant to deny is the cheapest way to remove it, and the gate will say so again the moment anyone wonders.
post_message.observed: 2026-08-07: zero invocations anywhere under apps/desktop/src/**, production or test.

reply_in_conversation.note: The non-streaming twin of stream_reply: same context assembly, same one-time-challenge -> governed_turn -> verify_and_record_receipt pipeline, differing only in delivery. Every chat surface uses the streaming sibling (services/desktop.ts streamReply), so the buffered variant has no frontend wrapper. It is kept because the governed pipeline it carries is the same audited one and a non-streaming caller (automation, a headless turn) is a plausible future consumer; until such a caller exists it is unreached by design.
reply_in_conversation.observed: 2026-08-07: zero invocations under apps/desktop/src/**; commands.rs keeps it on the governed path.

set_run_step_status.note: No surface authors a run-step status directly. Command.tsx drives steps through stream_run_step (the governed execution path, which sets status as a consequence of real work) and advance_run (which moves the run forward transactionally). A renderer that could stamp an arbitrary step status could claim a step succeeded without it having run, which is the exact honesty defect the six-surface work closed, so leaving this uncalled is the safer state.
set_run_step_status.observed: 2026-08-07: zero invocations under apps/desktop/src/**; add_run_step / advance_run / stream_run_step are the live callers of the run-step repo.

create_decision.note: An OPEN gap, declared rather than dressed up. The Decisions page is a read-only mirror today - it renders list_decisions plus the engine evidence-chain read - and offers no control that records a decision, so create_decision is registered and allow-granted with nothing invoking it. Two honest closures exist: wire a create control on the Decisions page, or flip the grant to deny because authoring governance decisions from the webview is not wanted. Until one is chosen this is invokable surface with no user.
create_decision.observed: 2026-08-07: zero invocations under apps/desktop/src/**; grant is allow-create-decision, policy tier L1.

assert_no_bytecode_shadow.reason: The worked example this gate was built around, and it CHANGED STATE while the gate was being written. Residual item O-1 (HIGH) is the canonical 'implemented and nothing calls it': the function exists, is documented, raises ProtectedScopeError for __pycache__/.pyc/.pyo under a digest root - and for the whole life of the repository had zero callers, so a forged .pyc could shadow a digest-verified .py and nothing noticed. It now has real callers on the wall's own path, so the expectation is must_have_caller and the gate protects those call sites: if either is refactored away the gate turns RED rather than the defect silently reopening. NOTE THE LIMIT - this proves the calls EXIST; it does not verify the rest of O-1 closure (hooks running python -B, compileall scoped off digest roots, the stray-.pyc regression test), and O-1's status in docs/PHASE_10_PRODUCTION_ITEMS.md is owned there, not here.

Both were UNCOMMITTED working-tree changes by a concurrent agent at the time of this run; the gate re-derives them every run, so a revert turns it RED.

head_anchor_payload.reason: The OWNER-FACING half of the anchor API. O-2's fix landed: `append` now assembles the anchor payload itself and refuses any document that is not a signature over exactly those bytes, via the private `_anchor_payload` this function also wraps. What stays caller-less in this repo is deliberate -- the caller is the owner's out-of-band signing command, reached through BRO_AUDIT_ANCHOR_SIGNER, and a key the ledger's own writer could reach would prove nothing. So this is an exported API with an external consumer, NOT dead code. It gains an in-repo caller only if a signing helper ships inside the engine, which would defeat the point.

attach_head_anchor.reason: The install half of the same owner-facing API: it verifies a signed anchor against the trusted registry and against the ledger's current chain before storing it. Caller-less in this repo for the same reason as `head_anchor_payload` -- the party holding the signing key is outside the engine by design. Not dead code, and not the O-2 gap: that gap closed when `append` started attaching an anchor and keyed `verify` started requiring one.

If the call site is removed or refactored away the gate turns RED, because losing it would silently return conductor identity to a plain environment-variable claim.

require_conductor_session_token.reason: A policy KEY, not a function, so `defined_in` is null and the flag is 'called' by being read. It is read through the named constant CONDUCTOR_SESSION_POLICY_KEY rather than as a bare literal, so the declaration states that one hop and the gate verifies the binding is real before following it - an undeclared indirection would otherwise read as zero readers. pull_output.reason: The rev-30 §4.10(f) DESKTOP pull loop: it drives the chunked read, reassembles into a bounded buffer, and applies the §4.6/§7.1 whole-output length+digest gate against the SIGNED envelope (never §4.10(e)'s TRANSPORT-ONLY echo of the same two values). FLIPPED from declared_unreachable to must_have_caller on 2026-08-12, on this gate's own instruction, when `apps/desktop/src-tauri/core/src/bin/ladder_output_pull.rs` gave it a real named caller. Read the flip precisely, because it does NOT say the pull is wired into the product. The caller is a CI PROOF DRIVER: a binary in the crate that owns the loop, built and run only by `engine/ci/live/run_ladder_turn.sh`, which drives one live §4.10(f) pull (and four negative controls) against the real supervisor from the real sidecar principal. It exists in this crate rather than beside the ladder because `pull_output` takes a `ReceiptEnvelope` and has no parameter for the expected length or digest - deliberately, so no caller can aim the gate at the transport echo - so a Python driver would have had to re-implement the loop AND the gate, which is the duplicate-implementation defect this repository has now found seven times. What the flip buys is the thing a declared_unreachable entry could not: this gate now turns RED if that driver is ever deleted, i.e. if the one thing that has ever exercised the loop end to end goes away. PRODUCTION IS STILL UNWIRED, and by the same two named blockers as before. (1) The subprocess spawn on the submit side is an injected seam (`governed_submit::SubmitTransport`) that no production code implements: the tree's one bridge-spawn seam, `governed_sidecar::GovernedSidecar`, is async tokio reached from the renderer-hosting app crate, while the broker binary is synchronous. (2) Nothing calls `governed_turn_submit_prepared`: the broker's one production `GovernedExecutor` (`broker/src/chain_executor.rs::ChainExecutor`) drives the same §4.10(a0)/(a)(b)(c)/(d) hops over DIRECT AF_UNIX and reads the recorder's output off the local filesystem with `std::fs::read(&report_path)` rather than through this egress at all - so even a delivered token would not by itself put the pull on the live path. Reconciling those two architectures is an Architect's call. Neither blocker is expressible as a rust_symbols entry, which is why they are written here.

governed_pull_output.reason: The async half of the same hop: it turns `governed_output_pull::OutputPull` into round trips over one-shot sidecar subprocesses, one per chunk, and maps a local sidecar failure to a TRANSPORT error rather than to one of the five stream reasons (4.10(f) P1-5). The pull needs an `output_stream_id`, and rev-30 4.10(f) permits exactly one source for it: the 4.10(e) `brops.governed-turn-result.v1` `signed` frame. That frame NOW HAS a supervisor-side producer - `engine/runtime/governed_acceptance.py::AcceptanceDriver`, which requires an OutputReadService and carries the minted token; it landed in this same tree from a concurrent change and was uncommitted when this entry was written, so read the citation as of that moment. 4.6's `bridge.governed-turn-result.v1` - the only frame that moves that token across the sidecar boundary - now EXISTS on both hops (2026-08-10): the re-framer in bridge/governed_turn_result_bridge.py and the strict parser in apps/desktop/src-tauri/core/src/governed_bridge_result.rs. What is still missing is one hop further out: 4.6 is the REPLY to 4.10(g)'s `bridge.governed-turn-submit.v1`, and 4.10(g) is NOT IMPLEMENTED - no submit branch in engine_sidecar._dispatch and no orchestrator that drives 4.10(a0)/(a)/(b)/(c)/(d) inside one one-shot subprocess - so nothing ever holds a 4.10(e) reply to re-frame, and wiring a caller today would still mean inventing a token, which is the single thing 4.10(f) says may never happen. The dependency is typed rather than described: `OutputStreamCapability` can only be built from a verified 4.9 envelope plus a 43-char token, so the day a 4.6 frame delivers one the compiler names every place it has to reach. A second, larger disagreement would survive fixing that: the broker's Linux execution (`broker/src/chain_executor.rs::LinuxGovernedExecution`) reads the recorder's output off the local filesystem with `std::fs::read(&report_path)` instead of through this egress at all, so even a delivered token would not by itself put the pull on the live path. It is deliberately NOT a `#[tauri::command]` and is absent from `generate_handler!`, because 4.10(f) requires the pull to be an internal backend helper that never round-trips the webview; an ai.rs test asserts both of those against the sources so the attribute cannot be added quietly. UPDATED 2026-08-12 (the §4.10(g) submit-frame WRITER): the sentence 'nothing writes a submit frame' is now HISTORY too. `prepare_governed_turn_v1b`, `PreparedGovernedTurnV1B`, `GovernedGenerationConfig` and `resolve_governed_generation_config_v1b` exist in `apps/desktop/src-tauri/core/src/governed_prepare.rs`, and `governed_turn_submit_prepared` exists in `core/src/governed_submit.rs`: it asserts the §4.10(g) cross-bindings, builds the `bridge.governed-turn-submit.v1` frame, and strict-decodes the §4.6 reply. It is the Rust half of the governed `SHA256(JCS(flat string->string object))` formula whose Python half already shipped, and it reproduces §4.10(g)'s printed digest 732b58634d0a83e9b7fdf1ca69db78df145bd9dd79ac8922fed3e79cf5faab22 byte-for-byte. What blocks a caller is now TWO named things rather than an absence. (1) The subprocess spawn is an INJECTED seam (`governed_submit::SubmitTransport`) and NO production code implements it: the tree's one bridge-spawn seam, `ai::governed_sidecar_call`, is async tokio in the renderer-hosting app crate and carries `engine_trust::apply`, while the broker binary is synchronous and does not depend on that crate; a second spawn implementation is the half-wired export that seam's own comment warns about. (2) Nothing CALLS `governed_turn_submit_prepared`: the broker's one production `GovernedExecutor` (`broker/src/chain_executor.rs::ChainExecutor`) drives the same §4.10(a0)/(a)(b)(c)/(d) hops over DIRECT AF_UNIX and spawns the recorder rather than a sidecar, and its `ProductionResolver` supplies the three artifact digests from static deployment config instead of from a prepared turn - so wiring the writer means reconciling two architectures for the same hops, which is an Architect's call and not this change's. The live-supervisor blocker above is unchanged. The `parse_frame` entry that used to sit beside these was DELETED in the same change, because `governed_turn_submit_prepared` gives it a real production caller and a stale `declared_unreachable` on live code is a lie this gate cannot catch - it matches `governed_bridge_result::parse_frame(`, and an inherent associated call reads as `BridgeTurnResult::parse_frame(`.

prepare_governed_turn_v1b.reason: The 4.10(g) v1b single-pass preparation: it validates and caps `system`/`history`, canonicalizes the generation-config OBJECT, computes all three artifact digests ONCE from the bytes that are actually sent, mints the `request_nonce` ONCE, and is the sole source of the pre-store request, the create-pending facts, the submit frame and the final `Expected`. FLIPPED from declared_unreachable to must_have_caller on 2026-08-12 when `broker/src/ladder_executor.rs` called it -- which is the whole substance of that change, because the path it replaced read `system_sha256`/`history_sha256`/`generation_config_sha256` out of `$BROPS_BROKER_CONFIG` and therefore attested the same three digests for every conversation the deployment ever ran. The arithmetic is a test, not a claim: `ladder_executor::tests::the_history_digest_follows_the_conversation_not_the_config` fails if the digest stops moving with the conversation. Same caveat as its sibling entry: a caller is not a reachable user path, and the three fail-closed refusals above it are unchanged.

resolve_governed_generation_config_v1b.reason: Resolves the five frozen generation-config fields from the environment into a validated `GovernedGenerationConfig`, which is the only way to obtain one and therefore the only way to reach `prepare_governed_turn_v1b`. FLIPPED from declared_unreachable to must_have_caller on 2026-08-12 with the two entries above, and for the same reason: `broker/src/ladder_executor.rs::LadderChain::run_verified` calls it once per turn so the config the challenge commits to is the config that was validated, rather than a digest copied from somewhere else. It is deliberately re-resolved per turn rather than cached at broker start: the five values are environment-supplied, and a cache would let a turn attest a profile the process no longer runs under.

governed_turn_submit_prepared.reason: The 4.10(g) submit hop: it asserts the four cross-bindings, writes the `bridge.governed-turn-submit.v1` frame, drives ONE one-shot sidecar through a `SubmitTransport`, and strict-decodes the 4.6 reply. FLIPPED from declared_unreachable to must_have_caller on 2026-08-12, on this gate's own instruction, when `broker/src/ladder_executor.rs::LadderChain::run_verified` gave it a real named caller inside the broker service -- the process 4.10(g)'s Principal binding names. Read the flip precisely. It does NOT say a user can reach a governed turn. The three refusals that hold that line are untouched and byte-identical: `commands.rs::governed_verification_unconfigured` still returns `Some(...)` unconditionally before the model is invoked, `connect_broker` still refuses off Linux, and `main.rs::build_governed_executor` still returns the fail-closed `UpstreamBlockedExecutor` whenever `$BROPS_BROKER_CONFIG` is absent, malformed, TCB-violating, missing a manifest, missing a conversation source, or unable to resolve the 2.6 sidecar principal -- which is every shipped install, because nothing in the product writes that config. (Updated 2026-08-12: 'or carrying an unresolved sidecar trust environment' was one of the refusals in that list and is now GONE, deliberately. That refusal was permanent rather than provisional -- the provisioned set's conductor-session token binds agent_id bro-000 / role bro, the CONDUCTOR's identity, and the broker is 0 role #2 -- and it was aimed at the wrong thing: the two frames this transport relays, `bridge.governed-turn-submit.v1` and `bridge.governed-turn-output-read.v1`, reach no reader of the five provisioned variables. The broker now passes `SidecarTrust::RelayFramesOnly`, whose door refuses any request whose own top-level `protocol` is not one of those two, before a process exists. Read the consequence precisely: the broker's ladder was previously unreachable UNCONDITIONALLY, and is now unreachable for the remaining config reasons above, which is every shipped install for the same reason as before.
